questions.stem: Which is the correct definition of cell respiration?

options.text: Taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide from the lungs
options.why: That's breathing, or gas exchange. Mixing them up is the most common way to lose this mark.

options.text: Controlled release of energy from organic compounds to produce ATP
options.why: Respiration happens in every living cell, and its purpose is making ATP.

options.text: Converting glucose into ATP so energy can be stored for later
options.why: ATP isn't a long-term store. Cells make it and spend it almost right away.

options.text: Breaking down glucose in the absence of oxygen to release energy
options.why: That's only anaerobic respiration. The definition has to cover aerobic respiration too.

questions.stem: Why is ATP described as an energy currency rather than an energy store?

options.text: It holds more energy per gram than lipids or carbohydrates
options.why: It's the opposite. Lipids and carbohydrates are the long-term stores.

options.text: It can only be made in the mitochondria of animal cells
options.why: Glycolysis makes ATP in the cytoplasm, and plants make ATP too.

options.text: It's used almost as soon as it's made, so little is kept
options.why: Cells spend ATP as fast as they regenerate it from ADP and phosphate, like cash rather than savings.

options.text: It releases energy only when combined with oxygen
options.why: ATP releases energy when its terminal phosphate is removed by hydrolysis. Oxygen isn't involved.

questions.stem: Where does glycolysis happen, and what is its net ATP yield per glucose?

options.text: In the cytoplasm, with a net gain of 2 ATP
options.why: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate in the cytoplasm. It doesn't need oxygen.

options.text: In the mitochondrial matrix, with a net gain of 2 ATP
options.why: The matrix is where the link reaction and the Krebs cycle happen. Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm.

options.text: In the cytoplasm, with a net gain of 4 ATP
options.why: Four ATP are made, but two were spent getting started, so the net gain is 2.

options.text: On the inner mitochondrial membrane, with a net gain of 36 ATP
options.why: That's closer to the whole of aerobic respiration. Glycolysis alone makes a net 2 ATP.

questions.stem: In anaerobic conditions in muscle, why is pyruvate converted to lactate?

options.text: Because there's no oxygen available
options.why: That's when it happens, not why. The mark is for the purpose, which is regenerating NAD.

options.text: To regenerate NAD so glycolysis can continue
options.why: Glycolysis needs NAD to accept hydrogen. Making lactate frees up NAD, so glycolysis keeps producing ATP.

options.text: To produce more ATP from each pyruvate
options.why: Making lactate produces no ATP. It only keeps glycolysis running.

options.text: To remove carbon dioxide from the cell
options.why: No CO2 is released when lactate forms in humans. That happens in yeast.

questions.stem: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?

options.text: Lactate only
options.why: Lactate is the product in humans. Yeast makes something different.

options.text: Ethanol and carbon dioxide
options.why: Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO2. That's what bread and brewing rely on.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.why: Those are the products of aerobic respiration.

options.text: Lactate and carbon dioxide
options.why: Lactate doesn't come with CO2. Yeast makes ethanol and CO2.

questions.stem: What happens to pyruvate in the link reaction?

options.text: It's decarboxylated and oxidized to form acetyl CoA
options.why: A carbon leaves as CO2, hydrogen goes to NAD, and what's left joins coenzyme A. This happens in the matrix.

options.text: It's reduced to lactate so NAD can be regenerated
options.why: That's what happens in anaerobic conditions in muscle, not in the link reaction.

options.text: It's split into two molecules of glucose in the matrix
options.why: Pyruvate comes from glucose, not the other way around. It loses a carbon here.

options.text: It's phosphorylated by ATP synthase to make ATP
options.why: No ATP is made in the link reaction. ATP synthase works in the inner membrane.

questions.stem: Which products does the Krebs cycle release?

options.text: Oxygen, glucose and water
options.why: Oxygen is used at the end of the electron transport chain, and glucose isn't made here.

options.text: Lactate, ethanol and ATP
options.why: Lactate and ethanol are anaerobic products. The Krebs cycle needs aerobic conditions.

options.text: Pyruvate, NAD and oxygen
options.why: Pyruvate enters the link reaction before the cycle. NAD is reduced here, not released.

options.text: Reduced NAD, reduced FAD and CO2
options.why: The cycle's oxidations reduce NAD and FAD, and its decarboxylations release CO2. A little ATP is made too.

questions.stem: What does the energy released along the electron transport chain do directly?

options.text: Phosphorylates ADP to make ATP
options.why: That's the trap. The chain's energy pumps protons. ATP synthase makes the ATP afterward, in chemiosmosis.

options.text: Pumps protons into the intermembrane space
options.why: That builds up a proton gradient across the inner membrane, which chemiosmosis then uses.

options.text: Splits oxygen molecules into atoms
options.why: Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain. The energy isn't used to split it.

options.text: Breaks glucose down into pyruvate
options.why: That's glycolysis, which happens in the cytoplasm.

options.text: Electrons pass along carriers in the inner membrane
options.why: That's the electron transport chain. Chemiosmosis is what happens to the protons afterward.

options.text: Protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase
options.why: Protons move down their gradient through ATP synthase, and that flow phosphorylates ADP to ATP.

options.text: Water moves across the inner membrane by osmosis
options.why: Despite the name, chemiosmosis isn't about water. It's the movement of protons.

options.text: Protons are pumped out of the matrix using ATP
options.why: The pumping is powered by electron transport, not ATP. Chemiosmosis is protons flowing back in.

questions.stem: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration?

options.text: It's used by ATP synthase to make ATP
options.why: That's the trap. ATP synthase uses the proton gradient. Oxygen isn't used to make ATP directly.

options.text: It oxidizes glucose directly in glycolysis
options.why: Glycolysis doesn't need oxygen at all.

options.text: It accepts electrons at the end of the chain
options.why: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor and forms water. Without it, the chain backs up and stops.

options.text: It's released as a product of the Krebs cycle
options.why: The Krebs cycle releases CO2, not oxygen.

questions.stem: Where is the electron transport chain located?

options.text: In the cytoplasm
options.why: Only glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm.

options.text: In the mitochondrial matrix
options.why: The matrix is for the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.

options.text: In the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.why: The cristae fold that membrane to give more surface for the chain and ATP synthase.

options.text: In the outer mitochondrial membrane
options.why: The chain is in the inner membrane, so protons get pumped into the space between the two.

questions.stem: Why do lipids release more energy per gram than carbohydrates when respired?

options.text: Lipid molecules are larger than carbohydrate molecules
options.why: Size isn't the reason, and "because they're bigger" gets no marks.

options.text: Lipids can be respired without any oxygen
options.why: It's the reverse. Carbohydrates can be respired anaerobically, and lipids can't.

options.text: Lipids are more reduced, with more hydrogen per carbon
options.why: More hydrogen means more reduced NAD and FAD, so more ATP from the electron transport chain.

options.text: Lipids are broken down faster than carbohydrates
options.why: Carbohydrates release their energy faster. Lipids release more of it per gram.
